stats.note_on_absence: Torah #133 (Likutay Moharan Vol. 1) opens with the verse 'וְאֹרַח צַדִּיקִים כְּאוֹר נֹגַהּ' (Proverbs 4:18) and develops a single extended analogy: the Tzaddik is like the sun — always shining — but the world (עוֹלָם הַזֶּה) acts like the earth that intercepts the sunlight, preventing people from seeing the Tzaddik's great light. The coin-before-the-eyes parable illustrates how even a small object, when placed directly in front of the eyes, can block perception of something thousands of times larger. The concluding practical teaching (the eitza edge in the dataset) is: with just a simple turning-away-of-the-eyes, a person can remove the world from before them and instantly behold the great light of Torah and the Tzaddikim. The Baal Shem Tov's cited teaching confirms this. None of the comparisons in the text are declared via bechina language (בְּחִינַת, הַיְנוּ, נִקְרָא). The sun IS the Tzaddik analogically, but this is the analogical device of the mashal — it is not declared as a bechina equivalence. The structure is purely eitza: world-blocks-vision → remove-world → vision-restored. The absence of bechina language is a genuine structural feature of this short, practically-focused teaching.
